nodes.statement: A self-reproducing program is one that outputs an exact copy of its own source code when compiled and run.
nodes.span: write a source program that, when compiled and executed, will produce as output an exact copy of its source.
nodes.status_reason: The reader can understand the definition of the problem as stated.

nodes.statement: Figure 1 provides an example of a self-reproducing program written in C.
nodes.span: Figure 1 shows a self-reproducing program in the C programming language.
nodes.status_reason: The reader can accept the reference to the figure as an example.

nodes.statement: A self-reproducing program can easily be generated by another program.
nodes.span: This program can be easily written by another program.
nodes.status_reason: The text asserts this property without deriving it from prior steps.

nodes.statement: A self-reproducing program can carry additional arbitrary code that will also be reproduced.
nodes.span: can contain an arbitrary amount of excess baggage that will be reproduced along with the main algorithm.

nodes.statement: The C compiler is itself written in the C programming language.
nodes.span: The C compiler is written in C.
nodes.status_reason: The reader can accept this factual claim about the C compiler.

nodes.statement: The C compiler contains code that interprets character escape sequences in a portable way.
nodes.span: interprets the character escape sequence. This is an amazing piece of code. It "knows" in a completely portable way
nodes.status_reason: The reader can accept this description of the compiler's capabilities.

nodes.statement: Because the compiler knows how to interpret escape sequences, it can recompile itself and maintain that knowledge.
nodes.span: The act of knowing then allows it to recompile itself, thus perpetuating the knowledge.
nodes.status_reason: Follows from the compiler being written in C and already possessing the code to interpret the sequences.

nodes.statement: To add a new escape sequence like "\v", one first modifies the compiler source code to include it.
nodes.span: alter the C compiler to include the sequence "\v" to represent the vertical tab character.
nodes.status_reason: A hypothetical step in modifying the compiler.

nodes.statement: Recompiling the modified compiler source with the existing compiler fails because the existing binary does not yet understand the new sequence.
nodes.span: since the binary version of the compiler does not know about "\v," the source is not legal C.
nodes.status_reason: Follows from the fact that the old compiler lacks the new escape sequence definition.

nodes.statement: The compiler is trained by temporarily using the decimal value of the new character in the source code.
nodes.span: We look up on an ASCII chart that a vertical tab is decimal 11. We alter our source
nodes.status_reason: A step taken to bypass the compiler's lack of knowledge.

nodes.statement: The existing compiler can successfully compile the source code that uses the decimal value.
nodes.span: Now the old compiler accepts the new source.
nodes.status_reason: Follows from using a standard decimal value instead of the unrecognized escape sequence.

nodes.statement: The resulting binary is installed as the new compiler, which can now compile the portable escape sequence.
nodes.span: install the resulting binary as the new official C compiler and now we can write the portable version
nodes.status_reason: A step to finalize the training of the compiler.

nodes.statement: A compiler can learn a new self-referencing definition by being told once through a temporary workaround.
nodes.span: You simply tell it once, then you can use this self-referencing definition.
nodes.status_reason: Follows from the successful training process described in the previous steps.

nodes.statement: The compiler is modified to deliberately miscompile source code when it matches a specific pattern.
nodes.span: modification to the compiler that will deliberately miscompile source whenever a particular pattern is matched.
nodes.status_reason: A step introducing a deliberate flaw into the compiler.

nodes.statement: A deliberate bug inserted into a compiler is called a Trojan horse.
nodes.span: Since it is deliberate, it should be called a "Trojan horse."
nodes.status_reason: A definition provided by the author.

nodes.statement: A bug is planted in the compiler to target the UNIX login command.
nodes.span: The actual bug I planted in the compiler would match code in the UNIX "login" command.
nodes.status_reason: A specific application of the Trojan horse method.

nodes.statement: The replacement code for the login command is designed to accept a specific known password in addition to the correct one.
nodes.span: miscompile the login command so that it would accept either the intended encrypted password or a particular known password.
nodes.status_reason: A step detailing the payload of the Trojan horse.

nodes.statement: Compiling the login command with this compromised compiler allows the attacker to log into the system as any user.
nodes.span: if this code were installed in binary and the binary were used to compile the login command, I could log into that system
nodes.status_reason: Follows from the login command being miscompiled to accept the attacker's password.

nodes.statement: A Trojan horse left in the compiler's source code would be easily discovered by anyone reviewing the code.
nodes.span: Such blatant code would not go undetected for long. Even the most casual perusal of the source
nodes.status_reason: The reader can accept that obvious malicious code in the source would be spotted.

nodes.statement: A second Trojan horse is added to the compiler to target the compiler's own source code.
nodes.span: adds a second Trojan horse to the one that already exists. The second pattern is aimed at the C compiler.
nodes.status_reason: A step to hide the first Trojan horse.

nodes.statement: The second Trojan horse uses a self-reproducing program to insert both Trojan horses into the compiler during compilation.
nodes.span: The replacement code is a Stage I self-reproducing program that inserts both Trojan horses into the compiler.
nodes.status_reason: A step detailing how the second Trojan horse operates.

nodes.statement: The modified compiler source is compiled to create a bugged binary, which is then installed as the official compiler.
nodes.span: compile the modified source with the normal C compiler to produce a bugged binary. We install this binary
nodes.status_reason: A step to bootstrap the compromised compiler binary.

nodes.statement: Once the bugged binary is installed, the malicious code can be removed from the compiler's source, and the binary will automatically reinsert it during future compilations.
nodes.span: remove the bugs from the source of the compiler and the new binary will reinsert the bugs whenever it is compiled.
nodes.status_reason: Follows from the compiler binary containing the self-reproducing Trojan horse that targets the compiler source.

nodes.statement: The login command remains compromised without any malicious code being visible in any source code.
nodes.span: the login command will remain bugged with no trace in source anywhere.
nodes.status_reason: Follows from the compiler binary silently inserting the bug into the login command and the compiler source being clean.

nodes.statement: Code cannot be trusted unless it was entirely created by the user.
nodes.span: You can't trust code that you did not totally create yourself.
nodes.status_reason: Follows from the demonstration that clean source code can produce compromised binaries if the compiler is untrusted.

nodes.statement: Reviewing or verifying source code is insufficient to protect against untrusted code.
nodes.span: No amount of source-level verification or scrutiny will protect you from using untrusted code.
nodes.status_reason: Follows from the fact that the malicious behavior is introduced by the compiler binary, not the source code.

nodes.statement: The Trojan horse attack demonstrated on the C compiler could be applied to any program-handling software.
nodes.span: I could have picked on any program-handling program such as an assembler, a loader, or even hardware microcode.
nodes.status_reason: Follows from the general nature of the attack described.

nodes.statement: Bugs introduced at lower levels of the software stack are increasingly difficult to detect.
nodes.span: As the level of program gets lower, these bugs will be harder and harder to detect.
nodes.status_reason: Follows from the assertion that the attack can be applied to lower-level programs like microcode.

nodes.statement: The actions of computer hackers are equivalent to vandalism, trespass, and theft.
nodes.span: The acts performed by these kids are vandalism at best and probably trespass and theft at worst.
nodes.status_reason: The author's moral judgment on hacking activities.

nodes.statement: Breaking into a computer system should carry the same social stigma as breaking into a physical house.
nodes.span: The act of breaking into a computer system has to have the same social stigma as breaking into a neighbor's house.
nodes.status_reason: Follows from the assertion that hacking is equivalent to trespass and theft.

nodes.statement: The media should treat computer hacking as a mundane crime rather than something to be glorified.
nodes.span: The press must learn that misguided use of a computer is no more amazing than drunk driving
nodes.status_reason: Follows from the assertion that hacking is equivalent to ordinary crimes like trespass and vandalism.
